what_it_does: Running a large language model (an AI that generates or understands text) requires constantly shuttling huge amounts of data between where it is stored and where the math is done — this back-and-forth is the main bottleneck slowing things down and wasting energy. The key insight here is to do the math right next to the memory instead of shipping data across a wire. This chip stacks a logic layer (the part that does arithmetic) directly on top of a dynamic RAM chip (the kind of fast-access memory storage used in most computers today) using a technology called 3D hybrid bonding, where the two layers are fused face-to-face with tiny copper connections. A centralized controller manages both the memory and the compute, and a dual-input/output scheme lets the chip flexibly switch between two common types of AI math operations — multiplying a matrix by a vector (used during single-token generation) and multiplying two full matrices together (used during batch processing of many tokens). By cutting the distance data travels, the design reduces energy use and increases throughput compared to conventional separate-chip architectures.
